title: Air India Nears $1.1 Billion Lifeline From Tata and Singapore Airlines
excerpt: The cash infusion would be tied to performance milestones as the carrier grapples with record $2.3 billion losses and political pushback in Singapore over the use of state funds.
body:
• Air India is close to securing ₹100 billion ($1.1 billion) from Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines, with funding tied to performance milestones and released in installments
  • The carrier reported record combined losses of $2.3 billion in fiscal 2026, more than double the prior year, as a deadly crash, airspace closures, and regional conflict compounded its challenges
  • Singapore opposition lawmaker Kenneth Tiong publicly opposed using state investor Temasek's funds to shore up Air India, filing a parliamentary question on the matter
  • Temasek backed Singapore Airlines' investment in a public letter, calling the turnaround a complex, multi-year undertaking not expected to be linear

Air India is close to securing ₹100 billion ($1.1 billion) in fresh financial support from its owners Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter. The funding would be conditional on the carrier hitting performance milestones and would be paid out in installments.

The capital injection would be proportional to the shareholders' stakes: Tata Sons owns 74.9% of Air India, with Singapore Airlines holding the remaining 25.1%. Neither Air India, Tata Sons, nor Singapore Airlines have publicly confirmed the terms, according to Skift.

Record Losses Drive the Need

The funding comes after a brutal fiscal year for Air India. The carrier and its budget arm Air India Express posted combined losses of approximately $2.3 billion in the year ended March 2026, more than double the $1.1 billion loss reported the previous year, according to Reuters. Revenue fell nearly 9% to $7.5 billion.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=uYbZhZ09Ia8

The scale of the losses reflects the convergence of several crises. A Boeing 787 Dreamliner accident that killed 260 people consumed management bandwidth for months, damaged the airline's public image, and drove up costs. Pakistan's airspace ban on Indian carriers disrupted major international routes, while the broader West Asia conflict increased fuel costs and created further operational headwinds.

Singapore Political Pushback

The funding request has drawn political scrutiny in Singapore. Kenneth Tiong, an opposition Workers' Party lawmaker, publicly urged that state investor Temasek's funds not be used to prop up Air India through Singapore Airlines, which Temasek majority-owns.

"I will not support, nor expect, any future use of Temasek's funds to prop up Air India via Singapore Airlines. If Singapore Airlines wants to continue its bet on Air India, it should do so on its own two feet."

— Kenneth Tiong, Singapore Member of Parliament

Tiong filed a question for oral answer in Singapore's parliament on September 8, asking the transport minister whether losses from Singapore Airlines' foreign associates have been assessed against the carrier's ability to provide essential domestic transport services.

Temasek and SIA Respond

Singapore Airlines said its board would "carefully consider" any requests for additional capital, weighing them against the group's other capital requirements and Air India's business strategy, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

Temasek, for its part, expressed public support. In a letter to Singapore's Business Times, Juliet Teo, joint head of portfolio development at Temasek Singapore, said the firm viewed Singapore Airlines' investment in Air India from a long-term perspective. "Efforts of this scale take time and are not expected to be linear," the letter read.

What Comes Next

Air India's multibillion-dollar transformation has been underway since Tata took control of the former state-owned carrier in 2022. Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran has said the turnaround could take up to a decade. Incoming CEO-designate Tewolde Gebremariam, who officially joins later this month, is expected to focus on bolstering the cargo business and addressing persistent maintenance problems, according to Bloomberg.

Within the Tata Group itself, the investment has drawn internal scrutiny. Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts that controls Tata Sons, has raised concerns over Air India's losses at several board meetings, Reuters reported.

For the Indian diaspora, which makes up a significant share of Air India's long-haul traffic to North America, Europe, and the Gulf, the financial infusion signals that the Tata Group remains committed to seeing the transformation through — even as the path to profitability stretches further into the future.
